questions.q: Name the Tamil Shaiva canonical collection formed by the hymns of Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar, and state the century in which it was compiled.
questions.a: The collection is the Tevaram, compiled in the 10th century CE. A wrong answer (e.g., "Nalayira Divyaprabandham" or "Periya Puranam") reveals confusion between Shaiva and Vaishnava canons or between the hymns themselves and the later hagiography that narrates the saints' lives.

questions.q: Why did the Nayanars' use of Tamil instead of Sanskrit represent a significant shift in religious access? Explain in two sentences.
questions.a: Tamil was the spoken language of ordinary people, including women and lower castes excluded from Vedic Sanskrit learning; by composing in Tamil, the Nayanars bypassed Brahmanical mediation and made Shiva devotion directly accessible. A wrong answer that only mentions "language change" without linking to social exclusion misses the core historiographical point about democratization of bhakti.

questions.q: Appar was originally a Jain monk. How does this background inform the tone of his hymns toward Jainism and Buddhism? Use a specific example from his verses.
questions.a: Appar's hymns contain fierce polemics against Jainism and Buddhism, calling them "false creeds" and celebrating Shiva's triumph over them — reflecting a convert's zeal and the competition for royal patronage. A student who says "he respected all religions" ignores the historical reality of sectarian conflict documented in the Tevaram and inscriptions.

questions.q: Compare the social backgrounds of the three Nayanars. How does their diversity support the historian's claim that the bhakti movement challenged caste hierarchies?
questions.a: Appar was a Vellala (cultivator) convert from Jainism, Sambandar a Brahmin child prodigy, Sundarar a Brahmin adopted by a royal family — together they span Brahmin, non-Brahmin, and royal circles, showing bhakti cut across varna. An answer listing only their names without social categories fails to demonstrate the analytical link between biographical diversity and caste critique.

questions.q: Evaluate the statement: "Chola patronage of the Nayanars was purely religious devotion." Provide two pieces of evidence to support your judgment.
questions.a: The statement is inaccurate. Evidence: (1) Chola kings consecrated metal images of the three saints in temples and included them in processions, visually aligning royal authority with saintly sanctity. (2) They sponsored the compilation and liturgical use of Tevaram to legitimize their rule in the Tamil cultural zone. An answer calling it "purely religious" ignores the political instrumentalization of bhakti documented in inscriptions.

questions.q: Construct a timeline (7th–10th centuries) placing the lives of Appar, Sambandar, Sundarar, the compilation of Tevaram, and Chola temple-building at Thanjavur. Explain one cause-effect link between two consecutive events.
questions.a: Timeline: Appar (early 7th c.), Sambandar (mid 7th c.), Sundarar (late 7th c.) → Tevaram compilation (10th c.) → Rajaraja I builds Brihadisvara Temple (c. 1010 CE). Cause-effect: The saints' hymns sanctified specific sites (e.g., Chidambaram), which later Cholas developed into imperial temples to anchor their legitimacy. A timeline with incorrect sequencing (e.g., Tevaram before the saints) shows failure to grasp the transmission from oral performance to textual canon to state architecture.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: The Nayanars were Tamil Shaivite poet-saints (6th–9th centuries CE) who composed devotional hymns in Tamil praising Shiva; the three most prominent — Appar (Tirunavukkarasar), Sambandar (______), and Sundarar (Sundaramurti Nayanar) — authored the Tevaram, the first seven volumes of the Tamil Shaiva canon, and their lives and songs shaped temple rituals, pilgrimage networks, and Chola royal patronage in South India.
Fill in the blank: Imagine you visit the ______ Temple at Thanjavur and see bronze images of three saints carried in procession — who are they and why do they matter?
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: Student can explain how the lives and hymns of Appar, Sambandar, and Sundarar transformed Shaivite worship in Tamil Nadu, analyze their critique of caste and rival traditions (Buddhism/Jainism), and evaluate the Chola state's use of their legacy for political legitimacy.
